lines.text: Four hundred years of sound, from the first operas of Italy to the stadiums of K-pop. This is the story of music, and the people who made it.
It begins with Claudio Monteverdi, whose opera L'Orfeo of 1607 is one of the oldest still staged, a bridge from the Renaissance into the Baroque.
In Venice, a violinist and priest named Antonio Vivaldi wrote hundreds of concertos, many of them played by the orphaned girls he taught.
George Frideric Handel was born in Germany but made his name in London, first with operas, then with grand oratorios and the Water Music.
That same year Johann Sebastian Bach was born. His fugues and concertos were half forgotten after he died, and are now the bedrock of Western music.
In 1725 Vivaldi published The Four Seasons, four concertos full of birdsong, storms and hunts, telling a story with instruments alone.
Joseph Haydn, working for decades for the Esterhazy family, wrote over a hundred symphonies and helped shape both the symphony and the string quartet.
In Dublin in 1742, Handel's Messiah was heard for the first time. Written in just weeks, it is still sung every Christmas and Easter.
Then came Mozart, a child performer who grew into the composer of more than six hundred works before his death at only thirty-five.
Ludwig van Beethoven carried music from the Classical age into the Romantic, and kept composing even after he lost his hearing.
In Vienna in 1787 Mozart wrote Eine kleine Nachtmusik, a little night music, whose opening tune almost everyone knows.
In his final year Mozart worked on a Requiem, a mass for the dead. He never finished it, and his pupils completed it from his sketches.
That same autumn The Magic Flute opened, a fairy-tale opera of a prince and a bird-catcher, just weeks before Mozart died.
Franz Schubert poured out some six hundred songs in a short life, and much of his music was only heard after his death at thirty-one.
In 1801 Beethoven wrote a piano sonata that opens softly and ends in a storm. Later, someone named it the Moonlight Sonata.
In France, Hector Berlioz wrote the Symphonie fantastique, a whole story told by orchestra, and a book on orchestration that composers still read.
Four short hammering notes open Beethoven's Fifth Symphony, first played in Vienna in 1808. It may be the most recognised music ever written.
Felix Mendelssohn wrote his Midsummer Night's Dream music as a teenager, and in 1829 brought Bach back to life by conducting his St Matthew Passion.
Frederic Chopin left Poland for Paris and wrote almost only for the piano, nocturnes, waltzes and mazurkas full of his homeland's dances.
Robert Schumann wrote songs, piano works and symphonies, and ran a magazine that championed young talent like Brahms.
Franz Liszt was the first superstar pianist, drawing huge crowds across Europe, and he invented the symphonic poem.
Richard Wagner wrote his own librettos and built a theatre at Bayreuth for his Ring cycle. His music was hugely influential, his writings antisemitic.
Born the same year, Giuseppe Verdi gave Italy Rigoletto, La traviata and Aida, and his music became linked with the fight to unite the country.
Clara Schumann toured Europe as a pianist for six decades, premiering works by her husband Robert and by Brahms.
In 1824 Beethoven's Ninth added a choir to the symphony for the first time. Its hymn to brotherhood is now the anthem of the European Union.
Johannes Brahms moved from Hamburg to Vienna and wrote symphonies in the Classical forms, earning a place beside Bach and Beethoven as the three Bs.
In Russia, Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky wrote Swan Lake, The Nutcracker and the 1812 Overture, melodies that made him the best loved Russian composer of his day.
Antonin Dvorak brought Bohemian folk rhythms into concert halls, and in New York wrote his Symphony From the New World.
Edvard Grieg gave Norway its own voice in classical music, drawing on folk tunes for his piano concerto and the music for Peer Gynt.
Giacomo Puccini wrote La boheme, Tosca and Madama Butterfly, still among the most performed operas in the world.
Gustav Mahler ran the Vienna Court Opera and wrote vast symphonies, little played at first, that later became central to the concert hall.
Claude Debussy cared more for mood and colour than strict form, in pieces like Clair de lune and La mer.
Sergei Rachmaninoff wrote sweeping piano concertos, then left Russia after the revolution and settled in the end in the United States.
Arnold Schoenberg pulled music away from the old keys and devised the twelve-tone method, before fleeing the Nazis for California.
Maurice Ravel, a master of the orchestra, is remembered above all for Bolero and his version of Pictures at an Exhibition.
Back in 1877, Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake had failed at its Moscow premiere. The version danced today came almost twenty years later.
Igor Stravinsky wrote The Firebird and The Rite of Spring, and kept changing his style for the rest of a long life.
Sergei Prokofiev gave us Romeo and Juliet and Peter and the Wolf, and returned from abroad to the Soviet Union in the thirties.
Tchaikovsky's Nutcracker, the tale of a girl and her Christmas toy, first danced in 1892, is now performed everywhere each December.
Dmitri Shostakovich wrote fifteen symphonies under Soviet rule. Denounced more than once, he is often heard as quietly speaking against Stalin.
In Paris in 1913 The Rite of Spring had the audience shouting in the hall. Its pounding rhythms changed music for good.
Now the age of records and radio. Frank Sinatra rose in the forties and reinvented himself in the fifties with albums built around a mood.
Chuck Berry's guitar riffs and songs of teenage life, like Johnny B. Goode, set the pattern for rock and roll.
In Italy, Ennio Morricone scored more than four hundred films, from The Good, the Bad and the Ugly to Cinema Paradiso.
Ray Charles, blind from childhood, blended gospel, blues and jazz into early soul with songs like What'd I Say.
John Williams would write the music of Star Wars, Jaws, E.T. and Harry Potter, the sound of a whole generation at the movies.
Johnny Cash, the man in black, mixed country, rock and gospel, and recorded hit live albums inside prisons.
Little Richard's fast, loud records like Tutti Frutti in the mid-fifties helped kick rock and roll into life.
James Brown put the rhythm first and helped create funk. His drum breaks would later be sampled again and again.
Elvis Presley mixed country, blues and gospel, and his fifties hits and television shows made him the face of rock and roll.
Far from the charts, Estonia's Arvo Part wrote slow, bell-like music, and for years was the most performed living composer in the world.
Philip Glass built music from repeating patterns and made minimalism popular in operas, symphonies and film.
Tina Turner found fame with Ike Turner in the sixties, then came back on her own in the eighties with What's Love Got to Do with It.
John Lennon co-founded the Beatles and wrote many of their songs with Paul McCartney, then spoke for peace until he was shot in 1980.
Bob Dylan brought poetry to folk and rock with Blowin' in the Wind and Like a Rolling Stone, and later won the Nobel Prize in Literature.
Aretha Franklin came out of the Detroit church to become the Queen of Soul, and the first woman in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
Jimi Hendrix played the guitar left-handed and made feedback sing. His career lasted just a few years, Woodstock among them.
From Jamaica, Bob Marley and the Wailers carried reggae around the world with songs of struggle and unity.
David Bowie changed his sound and his face again and again, from Space Oddity to Ziggy Stardust to Heroes.
Elton John and his lyricist Bernie Taupin have written songs together since 1967, from Your Song to Rocket Man.
Bruce Springsteen sang the lives of working people in songs like Born to Run, in marathon shows with the E Street Band.
Stevie Wonder signed with Motown as a child, and in the seventies played almost everything himself on albums like Songs in the Key of Life.
All this grew from rock and roll, born in the early fifties when rhythm and blues, country and gospel met the electric guitar.
And in the Bronx in the summer of 1973, a party thrown by DJ Kool Herc is remembered as the birth of hip hop.
Grandmaster Flash invented new ways to mix and scratch records, and with the Furious Five recorded The Message.
Prince, from Minneapolis, played most of the instruments on his records, and Purple Rain made him a star.
Madonna rose in the eighties with hits like Like a Prayer, and kept reinventing herself to become one of the best selling women in music.
Michael Jackson began as a child in the Jackson 5 and grew into the King of Pop, whose dancing and videos changed the music business.
In Liverpool, four young men became the Beatles. In ten years their songs and studio work reshaped pop and rock.
In California the Beach Boys sang in close harmony about surf and cars, and Brian Wilson's Pet Sounds inspired a generation.
The Rolling Stones began in London playing American blues, and have kept on touring for more than sixty years.
Whitney Houston's powerful voice gave her hit after hit, crowned by I Will Always Love You.
The Who played loud, smashed their guitars on stage, and wrote a rock opera called Tommy.
Pink Floyd moved from psychedelic rock to concept albums like The Dark Side of the Moon and The Wall.
Led Zeppelin's heavy, blues-based sound laid the foundations of hard rock and heavy metal.
In Brooklyn, a future rapper and businessman was born. Jay-Z would become one of the best selling and richest musicians in the world.
Queen, fronted by Freddie Mercury, mixed rock with opera, and their Live Aid set is still talked about.
Tupac Shakur became one of the best selling artists ever, before he was shot dead in Las Vegas at just twenty-five.
Missy Elliott made some of the most inventive videos in music, and became the first woman rapper in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
The Notorious B.I.G. told stories in rhyme like few others. He was killed in Los Angeles, six months after Tupac.
From Sweden, ABBA won Eurovision in 1974 with Waterloo, and their songs became a stage show and a film.
Detroit's Eminem, with his speed and his alter ego Slim Shady, became the best selling hip hop artist of all.
Hip hop itself, rapping over beats and samples, grew from Bronx block parties into one of the most popular kinds of music on Earth.
Lauryn Hill's solo album won five Grammys, album of the year among them.
From Dublin, U2 became one of the biggest touring bands in the world, and campaigned against poverty.
Kanye West's soul samples and shifting styles shaped hip hop across the 2000s and 2010s.
Back in 1979, Rapper's Delight by the Sugarhill Gang became the first rap hit across America, and brought hip hop to everyone.
Run-DMC took rap into the mainstream, and teamed up with Aerosmith on Walk This Way to reach rock radio too.
In 1981 MTV began playing music videos around the clock, and the video became the way to sell a song.
Beyonce rose with Destiny's Child and went solo in 2003, winning more Grammys than almost anyone.
Michael Jackson's Thriller arrived in 1982, a mix of pop, funk, rock and soul that became one of the best selling albums ever.
Trinidad-born Nicki Minaj, with her playful voices, became one of the best selling women in hip hop.
In 1984 Rick Rubin and Russell Simmons founded Def Jam in a college dorm, home to LL Cool J, Public Enemy and the Beastie Boys.
In the summer of 1985, Live Aid joined concerts in London and Philadelphia, watched around the world, to fight famine in Ethiopia.
Public Enemy's dense, noisy records, like Fight the Power, spoke out against racism.
In Los Angeles, N.W.A's Straight Outta Compton took gangsta rap to a wide audience, and stirred debate across America.
Canada's Drake would become one of the most streamed artists in the world.
At sixteen, the Korean singer BoA became a star in Japan, the first K-pop act to top the Japanese charts.
Compton's Kendrick Lamar won the Pulitzer Prize for Music, the first artist outside classical and jazz to do so.
Nirvana, led by Kurt Cobain, brought grunge into the mainstream with Nevermind in 1991.
Adele's big ballads made her album 21 the best seller of the 2010s in many countries.
Taylor Swift moved from country to pop, writing her own songs, and re-recorded her early albums to own them.
In South Korea, a polished, highly choreographed pop took off in the nineties. K-pop would grow into a global industry.
Ed Sheeran, with a guitar and a loop pedal, wrote Shape of You, for years the most streamed song of all.
From Staten Island, the nine rappers of Wu-Tang Clan made Enter the Wu-Tang, a landmark of hip hop.
Back in Seoul, Seo Taiji and Boys mixed rap, rock and dance in 1992, and Korean pop was never the same.
Puerto Rico's Bad Bunny took Spanish-language music to the top of the world's charts.
In 1995 SM Entertainment was founded in Seoul, and built the idol system of training young singers and dancers for years.
A year later SM formed H.O.T., the first idol group, whose fans started the culture of K-pop fandom.
Billie Eilish recorded her first album with her brother in a bedroom, and swept the main Grammys at eighteen.
In 2005 a small label called Big Hit was founded. As HYBE, home of BTS, it is now one of Asia's largest music companies.
Big Bang wrote their own songs and set the style of the late 2000s, led by G-Dragon.
Girls' Generation, nine members strong, became the nation's girl group with their song Gee.
In 2008 Spotify opened, nearly all recorded music for a monthly fee, and owning music files began to fade away.
In 2012 Psy's Gangnam Style, with its horse-riding dance, became the first video on YouTube to pass a billion views.
A year later Big Hit formed BTS, seven members singing in Korean who would top the charts in America.
Blackpink followed, the most followed music act on YouTube and the first K-pop group to headline Coachella.
In 2023 Taylor Swift set off on the Eras Tour, through every chapter of her music, the highest grossing tour ever.
And in 2025 an animated film about a K-pop girl group who hunt demons became Netflix's most watched film, its song Golden topping the charts.
From a Venetian orphanage to a streaming phone, music keeps finding new ways to reach us all.
